1.note: Yahweh is using **son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human being.” See the Introduction to Ezekiel for more information on this form of address. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST. See how you translated the same expression in [4:1](ta:04).

The point of this comparison is that just as **a knife of the barbers** is sharp enough to shave the hair off a person, so is the sharp **sword** that Ezekiel is to take. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Since it must be as sharp as a barber’s knife]

Shaving off the hair of his head and his beard was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed that Yahweh was going to bring shame and grief on the people of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in a footnote.

The term **balances of weight** describes a scale which is an instrument for measuring how heavy something is. If your readers would not be familiar with what balances of weight are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a device for measuring weight]

The pronoun **them** refers to the hair that Ezekiel shaved off his head and his beard. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and you shall divide the hair into portions]

2.note: A **third** means one part out of three equal parts.

The implication is that **the city** is not the actual city of Jerusalem but the model of the siege of the city of Jerusalem that Ezekiel was instructed to build. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers as in the UST.

Here, **a sword** represents the enemies who will threaten the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verse 12. Alternate translation: [and I will send enemies to pursue them]
The pronoun **them** refers to the third of the people symbolized by the portion of hair that Ezekiel scattered to the wind. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers as in the UST.

3.note: The implication is that these **edges** are part of the robe that Ezekiel was wearing, in which he could fold and tie the hairs. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the hems of the robe you are wearing]

4.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the fire itself. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [From that fire, flames will spread out]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the judgment that would come on all the Israelites were **a fire** that would spread out from the hair that Ezekiel burned. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [From it, destruction will spread out]
See how you translated this phrase in [3:1](ta:03). Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

5.note: Ezekiel is using the phrase **Thus says the Lord Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. Alternatively, you could leave this as part of what Yahweh himself said to emphasize his authority as in the UST.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the model that Ezekiel made of the city were **Jerusalem** itself. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [model represents for Jerusalem]

Here, **lands** represents the peoples who live in the surrounding countries. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and all around her are the peoples of other countries]

6.note: Here, **she** refers to Jerusalem which represents the people who live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But the people living in Jerusalem have rebelled]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by acting wickedly]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people who live in Jerusalem, whom Yahweh has just spoken of earlier in the verse as **she** referring to the city. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [For the people of Jerusalem have rejected my judgments]

The terms **my judgments** and **my statutes** mean similar things. Ezekiel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my laws]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people disobeying his commands as if these **statutes** were a path that the people could have **walked** along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my commands—they have not obeyed them]

7.note: Ezekiel is using the phrase **thus says the Lord Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. Alternatively, you could leave this as part of what Yahweh himself said to emphasize his authority as in the UST.
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **arrogance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you have been arrogantly disobedient]

Yahweh is speaking to the people of Jerusalem, whom he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to Ezekiel, who is listening to him, that he feels strongly about their arrogance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to Ezekiel about the people of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [Because of the arrogance of the people of Jerusalem, more than the nations that are all around them—in my statutes, they have not walked, and my judgments they have not done, and according to the customs of the nations that are all around them, they have not done]

7.q: בְּ⁠חֻקּוֹתַ⁠י֙ לֹ֣א הֲלַכְתֶּ֔ם וְ⁠אֶת־מִשְׁפָּטַ֖⁠י לֹ֣א עֲשִׂיתֶ֑ם
7.note: The word **you** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Jerusalem, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

7.q: וּֽ⁠כְ⁠מִשְׁפְּטֵ֧י הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֛ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר סְבִיבוֹתֵי⁠כֶ֖ם לֹ֥א עֲשִׂיתֶֽם
7.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “and according to the customs of the nations that are all around you, you have not done.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “and according to the customs of the nations that are all around you, you have done.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

8.note: See how you translated this same phrase in previous verse.

Yahweh is using the term *Behold me** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen! I myself am now your enemy]

From here through verse 12, **you** is singular because it addresses the city of Jerusalem which represents the people who live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against you people of Jerusalem]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **judgments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will sentence you to be punished]
Here, **the eyes** represents seeing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [while the nations watch]

9.note: If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the abominable things you have done]

10.q: אָב֞וֹת יֹאכְל֤וּ בָנִים֙ בְּ⁠תוֹכֵ֔⁠ךְ וּ⁠בָנִ֖ים יֹאכְל֣וּ אֲבוֹתָ֑⁠ם
10.note: Here the masculine terms **fathers** and **sons** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [parents will eat children in your midst, and children will eat their parents]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **judgments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will judge you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **remnant** of people who survive were seed that he would **sow** by letting the wind scatter it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will scatter all who are left of you in all directions]

11.note: Following the custom of his culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred, his own life. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [as surely as I live]

Ezekiel is using **the declaration of the Lord Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. Alternatively, you could leave this as part of what Yahweh himself said to emphasize his authority as in the UST.

The implication is that the people of Jerusalem made the temple unclean by bringing idols into it and worshiping them there. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you have brought idols into my sanctuary and so made it unclean]

The terms **abhorrences** and **abominations** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with all your utterly detestable practices]

11.q: אֲנִ֤י אֶגְרַע֙ וְ⁠לֹא־תָח֣וֹס עֵינִ֔⁠י וְ⁠גַם־אֲנִ֖י לֹ֥א & אֶחְמֽוֹל
11.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately twice in this verse, even though the verbs translated as **I will reduce** and **I will not spare** already include this meaning by themselves. He is doing that to emphasize his firm resolve to punish the people of Jerusalem without mercy. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself will reduce you, and my eye will not have pity, and even I myself will not spare you]

11.q: אֲנִ֤י אֶגְרַע֙ וְ⁠לֹא־תָח֣וֹס עֵינִ֔⁠י וְ⁠גַם־אֲנִ֖י לֹ֥א אֶחְמֽוֹל
11.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I myself will reduce you, and my eye will not have pity on you, and even I myself will not spare you]
This could mean: (1) that Yahweh will withdraw his presence as in the UST, or (2) that Yahweh will reduce the number of people. Alternate translation: [I will diminish your population]

Yahweh is using **my eye will not have pity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will not show compassion.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will not show you any compassion]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional as in the UST. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will certainly punish you without mercy]

12.note: The implication is that this third of the people corresponds to the third of the hair that Ezekiel burned in the fire. The actions carried out on each third of Ezekiel’s hair in 5:2, each symbolize what will happen to the people of Jerusalem. You could include this information throughout the verse, if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [A third of you, like the hair you burned in the fire, by the plague will die]
Throughout this verse, the word **third** means one part out of three equal parts.

Here, **the sword** represents the enemies who will attack and threaten to kill the people, and **fall** represents “die.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And a third will die all around you when enemies attack]
See how you translated this same phrase, “and a sword I will empty after them,” in 5:2. Alternate translation: [and I will send enemies to pursue them]

13.note: Yahweh is using the phrase **my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean his anger and **will be finished** indicates that the anger he felt will be spent or satisfied. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then my fury will be used up] or [Then I will no longer be angry]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional as in the UST.

Yahweh is using **my heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean anger. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will let my temper cool among them] or [and I will calm down from my anger among them]

The implication is that Yahweh will be satisfied once he has fully expressed his anger against the people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will be satisfied once I have fully punished them]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **jealousy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I want my people to be faithful to me]

14.note: Yahweh is using a singular **you** here and through verse 17 to address the city of Jerusalem and its people that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate that he feels very strongly about the destruction he is about to bring. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this entire section as modeled in the UST as if he were speaking directly to the people through Ezekiel about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [And I will make Jerusalem into a desolation],

If your language does not use nouns for the ideas of **desolation** and **reproach**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [into desolate ruins and into something scorned]

Yahweh is using **to the eyes of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the opinion of]

15.note: The terms **a reproach** and **a taunt** mean similar things. Yahweh is using these terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [an object of utter scorn]

The phrase **a warning and a horror** expresses a single idea. The word **horror** tells more about **warning**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a horrible warning]

Yahweh is using **with nose and with heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean “with anger.” Similarly, **with reprimands of heat** would mean “with angry rebukes.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with extreme wrath and angry rebukes]

The implication is that because Yahweh himself has said these things, they will certainly happen. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. This also occurs in verse 17. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, have said this will happen, and so it certainly will]

16.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the terrible effects of the famine that he would send were **arrows** that he would shoot at the people. (See Deuteronomy 32:23 for similar language used as threats of doom. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the deadly disasters of the famine]

Even though Yahweh is addressing the people of Jerusalem directly, he is speaking of them in the third person as **among them**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [among you]

16.q: בָּ⁠הֶם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר & לְ⁠מַשְׁחִ֔ית אֲשֶׁר־אֲשַׁלַּ֥ח אוֹתָ֖⁠ם לְ⁠שַֽׁחֶתְ⁠כֶ֑ם
16.note: The first pronoun **them** refers to the people of Jerusalem, while the second one refers to the **disastrous arrows**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [among the people of Jerusalem—those arrows will begin your destruction]

16.q: אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָי֣וּ לְ⁠מַשְׁחִ֔ית אֲשֶׁר־אֲשַׁלַּ֥ח אוֹתָ֖⁠ם לְ⁠שַֽׁחֶתְ⁠כֶ֑ם
16.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [which I will use to begin your destruction]

16.q: לְ⁠שַֽׁחֶתְ⁠כֶ֑ם וְ⁠רָעָב֙ אֹסֵ֣ף עֲלֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠שָׁבַרְתִּ֥י לָ⁠כֶ֖ם
16.note: The word **you** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Israel. Since the previous 2 verses used the singular pronoun**you**, you could choose to continue with singular here for consistency. Alternatively, if you chose to use the third person in the previous verses, you could continue to do so here for consistency as modeled in the UST.
See how you translated the similar phrase, “breaking the staff of bread.” in 4:16. Alternate translation: [and I will cut off your supply of food]

17.q: וְ⁠שִׁלַּחְתִּ֣י עֲ֠לֵי⁠כֶם רָעָ֞ב וְ⁠חַיָּ֤ה רָעָה֙ וְ⁠שִׁכְּלֻ֔⁠ךְ
17.note: The first use of the word **you** is plural but in the rest of the verse, the singular is used. If your language marks that distinction, you could choose to continue with singular throughout for consistency. Alternatively, if you chose to use the third person in the previous verses, you could continue to do so here for consistency as modeled in the UST.

Here, **blood** represents any kind of violent death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [violent death will pass through you]

Here, **sword** represents war or an attack by enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will cause your enemies to attack and kill you]
